summary: This standards-track memo describes how to carry real-time text conversation, as specified in ITU-T T.140, in RTP packets. It obsoletes RFC 2793 and describes a payload format for sending text on its own RTP session.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4103 defines how to send real-time text conversation in RTP packets. It uses sequence numbers to detect missing packets and can repeat recently sent text so a receiver can recover some lost content.

questions: how does rtp text redundancy work
what is the cps parameter in sdp
what clock rate does text/t140 use
subtitle: Carry real-time text conversation in its own RTP stream with optional redundancy.

tldr.problem: Real-time text needs to arrive in order and with little data loss, including when carried alongside other conversational media.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP payload carries T.140 text as UTF-8, while RTP sequence numbers detect loss and optional redundant generations repeat earlier text blocks.
tldr.outcome: The format supports separate text sessions, loss marking, reordering, and optional redundancy; it obsoletes RFC 2793.

today: RFC 4103 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2793. It defines the RTP payload format for T.140 text conversation.

sections.title: Text Conversation in RTP
sections.content:
RFC 4103 carries text conversation, as defined by ITU-T T.140, in RTP packets. Text is sent in a separate RTP session dedicated to text and may be used alone or alongside voice and video.

T.140 text is encoded as UTF-8 without extra framing. A payload contains one or more complete text elements, so a UTF-8 character is never split between blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: Each RTP packet carries a block of text encoded as UTF-8. A separate text stream can be synchronized with voice or video when the sessions share a clock.

sections.title: The Text Payload and RTP Header
sections.content:
The text/t140 payload contains one T140block and no additional payload-specific header. The RTP sequence number helps detect lost or out-of-order packets; the timestamp records an approximate text-entry time and uses a 1000 Hz clock.

The marker bit is set on the first packet in a session and should also mark the first packet after an idle period. Text/t140 is recommended as the only payload type in its RTP stream because loss detection depends on consecutive sequence numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: The RTP sequence number helps the receiver put text in order and find gaps. The timestamp uses a 1000 Hz clock but does not by itself identify packet loss.

sections.title: Recovering Text with Redundancy
sections.content:
When no other protection is selected, the RFC requires redundancy based on RFC 2198. The sender repeats earlier T140blocks in later packets, allowing a receiver to fill a gap if it receives a later packet containing the missing text.

Redundant blocks are sent in age order so their sequence numbers can be inferred from the RTP sequence number. A redundant block with a timestamp offset above 16383 must not be included.
sections.plainLanguage: A later packet can repeat earlier text. If a packet is lost, the receiver may use a repeated block to restore its place in the text stream.

sections.title: Buffering, Idle Periods, and Missing Text
sections.content:
Text may be buffered for up to 500 ms; 300 ms is recommended when no other conditions require a different value. After an idle period, new text should be sent promptly, and an empty T140block can mark the start of that idle period.

A receiver can detect gaps in RTP sequence numbers, use available redundant blocks, and wait up to 1 second for out-of-order packets. If text remains missing, it inserts a missing-text marker.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender balances a short delay against packet size by buffering text briefly. The receiver can reorder delayed packets, use repeats, and mark text that did not arrive.

sections.title: Limiting the Character Rate
sections.content:
The SDP parameter cps sets a maximum character rate. The value is treated as a mean over any 10-second interval, and the default is 30 characters per second.

A sender that receives this parameter must keep its character rate at or below the stated value. A receiver must still tolerate temporary higher rates because older implementations may not recognize the parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: The cps setting asks a sender to limit how quickly it sends characters. Receivers still need to cope with older senders that may not follow that setting.
